newsitem.title: USA: EPA deal puts spotlight on chip industry's green record.
newsitem.headline: EPA deal puts spotlight on chip industry's green record.

text.p: The semiconductor industry makes 220 billion chips a year, but uses hundreds of millions of gallons of water and produces tons of toxic gases and hazardous solid and chemical wastes, each day.

As a result, California's Silicon Valley, the birthplace of the semiconductor industry, has more hazardous waste sites, 28, eligible for federal cleanup funding "than any comparable area in the United States," according to the Environmental Protection Agency.

Through the years, toxins in the air within semiconductor fabrication plants at several companies were linked to exceptionally high miscarriage ratess, and workplace toxins are also at core of allegations in a lawsuit brought this year by cancer victims who worked at a New York state chip maker.
Such toxic byproducts of the semiconductor industry, include phosphine, diborane, arsine, sulphuric acid and nitric acid.

With the industry's record as a backdrop, the agreement reached last week between Intel Corp. and the EPA, giving Intel more autonomy on how it controls and monitors hazardous emissions from its Chandler, Ariz., chip making facility, has led some to worry about future regulation of the industry.

While the specific Intel agreement is praised for a number of reasons, such as Intel's agreement to recycle 65 percent of the fresh water it uses and cap overall emissions below current EPA limits, some people fear less favourable pacts will follow.
The EPA and Intel deal is a pilot project which, if successful, will become a model for environmental regulation in the semiconductor industry.

"We are very concerned about it. We think the community accountability provisions are very weak -- giving up EPA oversight. We are concerned it will become precedent that others will follow," said Ted Smith, president of the Campaign for Responsible Technology and the Silicon Valley Toxics Coalition.

"Historically, this industry has been given one special treatment after another by the government, basically because the new industry of microelectronics is so important," said Dr. Joseph LaDou, director of occupational and environmental medicine at the University of California at San Francisco Medical School.
LaDou has treated hundreds of patients burned by hydraflouride and other chemicals used in semiconductor plants since the 1970s, when he had a practice in Silicon Valley.
Semiconductor chips, the tiny brains behind all manner of computerized equipment, are made in an intricate layering process involving dozens of chemicals.
Because chips are now so small and hold so many etched transistors -- 5.5 million on a Pentium Pro, for instance -- their production is done in a sterile, dustless room called a "clean room."
Air in clean rooms circulates about 20 times an hour.

Some critics argue that while no one chemical typically used in semiconductor manufacturing is used in high enough concentrations to be dangerous, the accumulated array of chemicals and vapours in fast moving air is harmful.
The National Resources Defence Council believes Intel gets too much leeway in determining emission levels of individual wastes.
Furthermore, technology advances bring changes to the semiconductor manufacturing process about every two years, according to industry literature.

"It is just a steady progression of new chemicals. The technology changes so rapidly that people are always playing a game of catch-up and workers in the community are subject to a long term experiment," LaDou said.
He said the industry was thought of as a "clean industry" because it is light manufacturing, but in reality "it has grim occupational health statistics," he said.

So while its total workplace injury and illness record is relatively low, at 4.4 cases per 100 full-time workers compared with 12.2 cases per 100 full-time workers in all manufacturing, its workplace illness rate appears relatively high. Workplace illnesses make up 26.7 percent of all the workplace injuries and illnesses suffered by semiconductor workers as of 1994.

The semiconductor industry has corrected some of its more grievous environmental misdeeds. For instance manufacturers have stopped using the underground storage tanks that leaked and caused the Superfund sites and most of those sites are in clean-up stages. Also, most manufacturers have stopped using chloroflurorocarbons after it was found they were burning a huge hole in the ozone layer.
The industry sponsored studies of the miscarriage problem among production workers and then most manufacturers stopped using the glycol ethers thought to lead to miscarriages.
